citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Core Concepts and Mental Model
citations.excerpt: Python's built-in `range()` function generates integer sequences lazily using half-open interval semantics: `[start, stop)`.

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
citations.excerpt: Off-by-one inclusive stop error: Learners often assume `range(1, 5)` includes `5`. In Python, the `stop` boundary is always exclusive. To include `5`, write `range(1, 6)`.

citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Core Concepts and Mental Model
citations.excerpt: Tracing a loop means constructing a step-by-step state table tracking every mutable variable before iteration 1, at the end of every pass through the loop body, and immediately after loop termination.

citations.title: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression)
citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
citations.excerpt: Off-by-one inclusive stop error: Learners often assume `range(1, 5)` includes `5`. In Python, the `stop` boundary is always exclusive. To include `5`, write `range(1, 6)`.

citations.excerpt: Python's built-in `range()` function generates integer sequences lazily using half-open interval semantics: `[start, stop)`.

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
citations.excerpt: Off-by-one inclusive stop error: Learners often assume `range(1, 5)` includes `5`. In Python, the `stop` boundary is always exclusive. To include `5`, write `range(1, 6)`.

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Difficulty Progression and Worked Examples
citations.excerpt: Easy: `list(range(4))` -> `[0, 1, 2, 3]`; `list(range(2, 6))` -> `[2, 3, 4, 5]`. Focus on inclusive `start` vs exclusive `stop`.

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)
citations.label: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`) — Prerequisite Connections
citations.excerpt: Root Skill: `range_boundaries` has no prerequisites and directly underpins `loop_tracing`, `accumulator_initialization`, and `list_indexing`.

citations.title: Range Boundaries (`range(start, stop, step)`)

citations.title: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression)
citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Core Concepts and Mental Model
citations.excerpt: Tracing a loop means constructing a step-by-step state table tracking every mutable variable before iteration 1, at the end of every pass through the loop body, and immediately after loop termination.

citations.title: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression)
citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Common Misconceptions and Pitfalls
citations.excerpt: Skipping the last or first state row: Jumping directly from `i = 0` to `stop` causes off-by-one arithmetic mistakes. Always evaluate `stop` exclusivity before entering an iteration.

citations.title: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression)
citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Prerequisite Connections
citations.excerpt: Depends on: `range_boundaries` (you must know the exact sequence visited by `for` loops before you can trace body state accurately). Feeds into: `accumulator_initialization` and `conditional_evaluation`.

citations.title: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression)
citations.label: Loop Tracing (`for` and `while` State Progression) — Difficulty Progression and Worked Examples
citations.excerpt: Easy: Single variable increment inside `range(3)` with `print(count)` after loop. Trace `i=0 -> count=1`, `i=1 -> count=2`, `i=2 -> count=3`.
